topic.title: Help
topic.text: This [window](Windows) does not have a specific help topic of its own. See [Help On Help](Help On Help) for how to find your way around, or pick one of the topics from the table of contents.

topic.title: Help On Help
topic.text:
The #{help} system is itself a [window](Windows), so everything you know about moving and closing windows works here too. Press F1 at any time to open help for whatever you are currently doing.
Words shown in a different colour are #{links}. Press Tab and Shift-Tab to move between the links on a page, then press Enter to follow the one that is highlighted; you can also click a link with the mouse. Use the arrow keys, Page Up, and Page Down to scroll through a topic that is longer than the window.
Every topic is listed in the #{table of contents}, and important terms are gathered in the #{index}; both are reachable from the help window so you can jump straight to what you need. When you are finished, close the help window with Ctrl-W or its close box, the same as any other [window](Windows).
See also [Menus](Menus) and [Windows](Windows).

topic.title: Menus
topic.text:
#{Menus} run along the top of the screen and group related commands together. Open a menu by clicking its title with the mouse, or press Alt plus the highlighted letter in the menu title (for example, Alt-F opens the File menu).
Once a menu is open, use the up and down arrow keys to move between items and press Enter to choose one. The left and right arrow keys move to the neighbouring menu. Press Escape to close the menu without choosing anything.
Many menu items show an #{accelerator} key on the right, such as Ctrl-X or F2. You can press that key at any time to run the command directly, without opening the menu first.
Items that are dimmed are not available right now; they usually become active once a [window](Windows) of the right kind has focus.
See also [Windows](Windows) and [Help On Help](Help On Help).

topic.title: Windows
topic.text:
#{Windows} in this toolkit follow the classic DOS-style pattern: framed, overlapping panels driven mostly from the keyboard. If you have only ever used windows you swipe or click, the ideas will be familiar but the controls below are worth a quick read.
Several windows can be open at once, stacked on top of one another. The one in front is the #{active window} and is where your keystrokes go; its border is drawn differently so you can tell it apart from the rest.
To move a window, drag its title bar with the mouse, or press Ctrl-F6 to enter keyboard move/resize mode and use the arrow keys. To resize a window, drag its lower-right corner, or use the arrow keys while in move/resize mode and press Enter when you are done.
Each window has controls on its border. The box in the upper left closes the window; the marks in the upper right maximize or restore it. You can also close the active window with Ctrl-W.
When several windows are open, press Alt-Tab (or F6) to cycle the active window from front to back, and Shift-Alt-Tab (or Shift-F6) to cycle the other way. Windows can also be tiled or cascaded from the Window menu so they no longer overlap.
Some windows hold a different kind of content and have their own help: see [Editing Text](Editing Text), [Editing Tables](Editing Tables), and [Terminal Window](Terminal Window).
See also [Menus](Menus) and [Help On Help](Help On Help).

topic.title: Editing Text
topic.text:
The #{text editing} [window](Windows) lets you enter and change text directly. Type to insert characters at the blinking #{cursor}, and use Backspace and Delete to remove the characters before and after it.
Move the cursor with the arrow keys. Home and End jump to the start and end of the current line; Page Up and Page Down scroll by a screenful; and Ctrl-Home and Ctrl-End jump to the very beginning and end of the document.
Hold Shift while moving the cursor to #{select} text. Selected text can be cut with Ctrl-X, copied with Ctrl-C, and pasted with Ctrl-V. You can also select text by dragging with the mouse. Use Ctrl-Z to undo the last change and Ctrl-Y to redo it.
See also [Editing Tables](Editing Tables) and [Windows](Windows).

topic.title: Editing Tables
topic.text:
A #{table editing} [window](Windows) arranges data into rows and columns of #{cells}. One cell is highlighted as the current cell; this is where typing and editing take place.
Move between cells with the arrow keys. Tab and Shift-Tab move right and left, and Enter moves down to the next row. Home and End jump to the first and last cell in the current row, and Page Up and Page Down move a screenful of rows at a time.
To change a cell, simply move to it and begin typing, then press Enter to commit the new value or Escape to cancel and keep the old one. Columns can be widened or narrowed by dragging their borders with the mouse.
See also [Editing Text](Editing Text) and [Windows](Windows).

topic.title: Terminal Window
topic.text:
A #{terminal window} runs a real command-line #{shell} or program inside a [window](Windows). Whatever you type goes straight to that program, and its output appears in the window, just as it would in a full-screen terminal.
Because your keystrokes belong to the program, the usual window shortcuts are handed through to it instead. To move or resize the terminal from the keyboard, use the window's border controls or the move/resize mode described under [Windows](Windows).
The window scrolls as new output arrives; use Page Up and Page Down to look back over earlier output. When the program you started finishes, the terminal shows that it has exited, and depending on how it was opened the window may close on its own.
See also [Windows](Windows) and [Menus](Menus).
